inline.s: Think about it seriously: why do you have birth and death? For what cause did you enter your mother’s womb? For what cause do you drown in craving and the entanglement of love? For what cause do you wish to escape saṃsāra? For what cause do you wander abroad in every direction? For what cause do you call upon and visit spiritual benefactors? For what cause do you tread famous mountains and climb blessed lands? You pass through the monastery groves, cross the villages, go to Nanhai this year, roam Mount Wutai next year, visit Mount Emei the year after — even if you travel the whole world over, even if you pass through dust-mote kalpas, exhausting lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, and serve the great spiritual benefactors of the ten directions, still you never get beyond the gate of illusion; and so this is not the ultimate, true place.

[Drowning (gǔ)] To be buried and lost, to sink. [Entanglement of love] The Yoga Sutra says: “Craving that arises inwardly and outwardly, within the activity of love — one should know its mark; this is called the defilement of the entanglement of love.” [Beyond the ordinary sphere] This uses the allusion “his traces filled the land, yet his aspiration transcended the ordinary sphere,” meaning: his feet covered the four seas, his mind transcended the dusty world. The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wude of Fenyang says: “If one does not advance, there can be no natural Śākyamuni or natural Maitreya; therefore set out beyond the ordinary sphere and enter the stairway of the sages.” [Protective society] A kind of folk organization in old rural villages; because it was established on the basis of the bao (the hundred-household unit), it was called a protective society. [Within the realm] The world, all under heaven. [Dust-mote kalpas] That is, “dust-mote kalpa” or “three-thousand dust-mote kalpa,” meaning: grind all things within three thousand great thousand-worlds into ink, and every time one passes through a three-thousand great thousand-world, let fall one drop; when the ink is gone, all the worlds passed through are again shattered into motes of dust, and each mote of dust is counted as one kalpa — this is a simile for an extremely long span of time.

[Yet though it be so, this is called mistaking the head and clutching at its reflection. There is no harm in going home along the road one came; if one can cut through the knot of illusion with a single step, then the boundless net of illusion is in one instant rent asunder; the shoreless ocean of illusion is in one instant dried up; the measureless karma of illusion is in one instant dissolved; the boundless practices of illusion are in one instant attained; the measureless beings of illusion are in one instant ferried across. This is what is called practicing illusion by means of illusion — as it is said, the illusory mind of sentient beings is still extinguished in dependence on illusion. If it be otherwise, then even though one pass through three lives and sixty kalpas, with Mañjuśrī as father, Avalokiteśvara as mother, and Samantabhadra as teacher, and would rely on these intimate causes to seek the matter of escaping birth and death, one is far, far away! Consider this well; do not say that I am a phantom person and that what I speak are not true words. Investigate! Investigate!]

Though you toil and rush about in this way, worn out in body and mind, it is still called “mistaking the head and clutching at its reflection, running madly without cause,” and it is not the ultimate, true place. You ought rather to go home along the road you came (and not toil and rush about seeking spiritual benefactors); if you can go home along the road you came (doing the work right where your mind stirs and thoughts arise) and cut through the knot of illusion with a single step, then the boundless net of illusion is in one instant rent asunder; the shoreless ocean of illusion is in one instant dried up; the measureless karma of illusion is in one instant dissolved; the boundless practices of illusion are in one instant attained; the measureless beings of illusion (illusory sentient beings) are in one instant ferried across. This is what is called practicing illusion by means of illusion — as it is said, “the illusory mind of sentient beings is still extinguished in dependence on illusion.” If you do not practice thus (going home along the road you came, cutting through the knot of illusion), then even though you pass through three lives and sixty kalpas, with Mañjuśrī as father, Avalokiteśvara as mother, and Samantabhadra as teacher, and would rely on this intimate cause to settle birth and death, that is far, far indeed! You must earnestly ponder these principles, and on no account think that I am a phantom person and that what I speak are not true words. Investigate! Investigate!

The Chan practicer Zhenyu placed his hopes for his own cultivation and realization upon spiritual benefactors; and so, sparing himself no hardship, he roamed the four seas and visited famous teachers everywhere. Master Hanshan, taking the verse of Viśvabhu Buddha that he had brought to ask about, instructed him with the samādhi of illusion, telling him to go home along the road he came (doing the work right where his mind stirs and thoughts arise) and to cut through the knot of illusion. And he especially roused him, saying: to say nothing of famous teachers and great spiritual benefactors — even if you relied on the intimate causes of Mañjuśrī as father, Avalokiteśvara as mother, and Samantabhadra as teacher in order to escape birth and death, that would be utterly impossible; only by doing the work yourself right where your mind stirs and thoughts arise, and cutting through the knot of illusion, can you escape birth and death.

[Mistaking the head and clutching at its reflection] To lose one’s own head and take up the reflection in a mirror instead. It is a metaphor for losing one’s true nature and failing to see one’s own original face. This uses the simile recorded in the Śūraṅgama Sūtra

Fascicle Four: In the city of Śrāvastī there was a man named Yajñadatta who one day looked at his face in a mirror, and, seeing in the mirror the brows and eyes of his own head, was delighted; but when he turned to look at his own head, he could not see the brows and eyes, and so gave rise to great rage, thinking himself possessed by a demon, and thereupon ran madly about without cause. Here one’s own head is a simile for the true nature, and the head in the mirror a simile for delusive appearance. Delight at seeing brows and eyes on the head in the mirror is a simile for falsely seizing the illusory state as real and clinging to it without letting go; rage at one’s own head for not showing brows and eyes is a simile for delusion and falsehood turning away from the true. The Five Lamps Meeting at the Source

Chan Master Hongying of Letan says: “The patriarchs succeeded one another, until Bodhidharma came from the West, pointing directly at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming Buddha, setting up no reliance on words or language — was this not the ancient sages’ skillful means? Yet people today do not believe it; instead they mistake the head and clutch at its reflection, running wild upon a mad path, so that they are left utterly alone (líng píng, solitary and shadowless), wandering through birth and death.” Master Hanshan here uses this allusion to point out the error of the Chan practicer Zhenyu, who did not do the work right where his own mind stirs and thoughts arise, but sought the Dharma outside the mind and rushed about in all directions. [Going home along the road one came] The Old Man Wansong says: “If one can go home along the road one came, one turns about and returns to the father. Do you not see the saying: a single thought turned back to the light is the same as attaining the original.” [Knot of illusion] A knot means binding; it is another name for affliction. Because affliction can bind the body and mind of sentient beings so that they cannot be freed but forever sink into birth and death, it is called a “knot.” The knot of illusion means that the knot is an illusion. [Three lives and sixty kalpas] The time required by the Śrāvaka Vehicle to cultivate and realize the fruit. The quickest realize the highest fruit in three lives; the slowest realize the highest fruit in sixty kalpas.

blocks.text: 13. The Wondrous Practice of Freedom from Desire

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Practicer Ruoliang)

[The Buddha said: “To shave off the beard and hair and become a śrāmaṇera, to be free of desire and still — this is foremost.” From this we know that desire is the foremost great matter at the head of the road of birth and death. Therefore he sharply rebuked it and strictly warned against it; being free of it, one attains peace
(the same character as “steady”)
and happiness. The reason sentient beings sink into the sea of suffering and cannot quickly reach the other shore is none other than the fault of desire.]

The Buddha said: “To shave off the beard and hair and become a śrāmaṇera, to be free of desire and still — this is foremost.” From this we know that desire is the foremost great matter at the head of the road of birth and death. Therefore the Buddha sharply rebuked it and strictly warned against it; being free of desire, one attains peace and happiness. The reason sentient beings sink into the sea of suffering and cannot quickly reach the other shore is entirely the fault of desire!

[The Buddha said: “The cause of all suffering is craving, which is the root.” If craving is extinguished, there is nothing to rely on. Moreover, the three realms are the house in which all sentient beings take refuge, and desire is its foundation. The clamor of the dust of affliction — all of it is this making noise. If one once departs from this reliance, then there is no longer any question of breaking the three poisons, leaving the three realms, and shattering the net of Māra; at such a time the Tathāgata is greatly delighted. From this we know that if the five desires are not abandoned, the three realms are hard to break, and our Tathāgata’s sorrow may be known; to seek still liberation will be difficult.]

The Buddha said: “The cause of all suffering is craving, which is the root.” If craving is extinguished, then suffering has nothing to rely on. Moreover, the three realms are the house in which all sentient beings take refuge, and desire is its root. The reason why affliction clamors and disturbs, so that one cannot be still, is entirely because of desire! Once desire is let go, affliction and all suffering have nothing to rely on, and then there is no longer any question of breaking the three poisons, leaving the three realms, and shattering the net of Māra; at such a time the World-Honored One is greatly delighted. From this we know that if the five desires are not abandoned, the three realms are hard to break, and our Buddha’s sorrow may be known; and to seek still liberation will be difficult!

[Foundation] Basis, root. [Dust of affliction] The mind toiling over the objects of dust — another name for affliction. [Five desires] Form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. Form means beautiful appearances; sound means melodious voices; fragrance means fragrant scents; taste means delicious flavors; touch means pleasant sensations of the body. These five can cause the mind of craving to arise, and so they are called the five desires.

[Ruoliang left home young and wandered on pilgrimage in many places. Now he has met this old man, aroused the bodhi mind, and received the śrāmaṇera precepts. To resolve to cultivate the practice of freedom from desire — this is the foremost wondrous practice of one who wishes to escape birth and death. The only fear is that the resolve be unsteady and the practice lacking in strength. The Buddha said: “Only after long endurance of hardship can one attain it.” One should settle a firm resolve and not stop until one has become Buddha; this is truly resolving to cultivate the practice of freedom from desire.]

Ruoliang left home young and wandered on pilgrimage in many places. Now he met this old man, aroused the bodhi mind, and received the śrāmaṇera precepts. To resolve to cultivate the practice of freedom from desire — this is the foremost wondrous practice of one who wishes to escape birth and death. But out of fear that his resolve might be unsteady and his practice lacking in strength, the old man gave the instruction above. The Buddha said: “Only after long endurance of hardship can one attain it.” Therefore one should settle a firm resolve and not stop until one has become Buddha; this is truly resolving to cultivate the practice of freedom from desire.
(The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Practicer Fajin)

[Fajin said of himself that his nature had much habit of anger; the old man therefore tamed him by skillful means and showed him the Dharma gate of patience. He further instructed him, saying: Master Yongjia has said: “My teacher saw the Lamp-Lighting Buddha; for many kalpas he was the Patient Immortal.” From this we know that the single practice of patience is the foremost wondrous practice for becoming Buddha.]

Fajin said of himself that the habit of anger was very heavy; the old man (Master Hanshan referring to himself) therefore tamed him by skillful means and showed him the Dharma gate of patience. He further instructed him, saying: Master Yongjia says in the Song of Realizing the Way: “My teacher saw the Lamp-Lighting Buddha; for many kalpas he was the Patient Immortal.” From this we know that the single practice of “patience” is the foremost wondrous practice for becoming Buddha.

[Therefore our teacher, the old Śākyan, life after life was slandered and harmed by Devadatta, down to his appearance in this present life. Devadatta’s various devices to destroy the Dharma stopped at nothing, and more than once he even tried to take his life. Yet at the Lotus assembly the Buddha predicted for him that he would become a Buddha, saying: my thirty-two marks and eighty excellences, my supreme and wondrous virtues, were all brought to accomplishment through the good friend Devadatta. Was this not because the single practice of patience is an essential practice for becoming Buddha? He also said: formerly, when King Kali cut my body to pieces, at that time I had no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life; if I had had the mark of a self, of a person, of a being, or of a life, the Lamp-Lighting Buddha would not have given me the prediction.]

Therefore our World-Honored One, life after life, was slandered and harmed by Devadatta, down to this present life. Devadatta’s various devices to destroy the Dharma stopped at nothing, and more than once he even sought to take the World-Honored One’s life. Yet at the Lotus assembly the World-Honored One predicted for him that he would become a Buddha, and said: the reason I have realized the thirty-two marks and eighty excellences, my supreme and wondrous virtues, is that they were brought to accomplishment through the persecution of the good friend Devadatta. Does this not show that the single practice of “patience” is an essential practice for becoming Buddha? The World-Honored One also says in the Diamond Sūtra: formerly, when King Kali cut my body to pieces, at that time I had no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life; if I had had the mark of a self, of a person, of a being, or of a life, the Lamp-Lighting Buddha would not have given me the prediction.

[Devadatta] The Buddha’s cousin, who left home and studied supernormal powers; his body bore thirty marks. He persecuted the Buddha again and again. [My teacher saw the Lamp-Lighting Buddha; for many kalpas he was the Patient Immortal] The World-Honored One (my teacher) came to see the Lamp-Lighting Buddha and receive the prediction of becoming a Buddha, all because of the tempering he underwent through many kalpas as the Patient Immortal. Utterly contrary to worldly people, the Buddha took being humiliated as a good thing, for only through a hundred refinings does iron become steel, and only through patience can the marks of self, person, being, and life be worn away — as it is said, “hardship and adversity bring you to completion.” [Seeing the Lamp-Lighting Buddha] In the past, when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva of the seventh ground, he met the Lamp-Lighting Buddha and heard the Dharma, realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, and rose to the eighth ground; the Lamp-Lighting Buddha then gave him the prediction, saying: after ninety-one kalpas, in the kalpa called Bhadra, you shall become a Buddha with the name Śākyamuni. [Prediction] The Buddha’s advance naming of a bodhisattva: after how many ages, in such-and-such a place, in such-and-such a country, one will become what Buddha. [Bhadra kalpa] The past great kalpa is called the Adornment kalpa, the future great kalpa is called the Constellation kalpa, and the Bhadra kalpa is the present great kalpa; because a thousand Buddhas appear in this great kalpa, it is called the “Bhadra kalpa.”

[From this we see: for all sentient beings, the implements of the suffering of birth and death are all accomplished through having a self; the unsurpassed bodhi, the adornment of merit and wisdom, is all reached through having no self. Because the self is set in opposition to things, right and wrong arise; right and wrong arising, love and hate are established; love and hate established, joy and anger proliferate; the self-nature grows turbid and the mind-ground grows dim; the mind-ground dim, all evils grow; all evils growing, all suffering gathers; all suffering gathered, birth and death are prolonged! All of this is brought about by the self. How grave is the harm done by the self! It is like a heavily fortified city with strong soldiers — how could it be broken easily?]

From this we see: the reason all sentient beings have birth, death, and suffering is that these are established through having a self; the unsurpassed bodhi, the adornment of merit and wisdom, is all realized through having no self. Taking the self as the center, one stands opposed to others, and so right and wrong arise; right and wrong arising, love and hate are established; love and hate established, joy and anger breed. Then the self-nature grows turbid and the mind-ground grows dim; the mind-ground dim, all evils grow; all evils growing, all suffering gathers; all suffering gathered, birth and death roll on without end! All of this is brought about by the presence of a “self.” How grave is the harm done by the self! Yet to break the attachment to self is like attacking a fortress closely guarded by picked troops — how could it be broken easily!

[Having a self] To take the physical body (the four great elements) as one’s own body and thoughts (the shadowy reflections of the six dusts) as one’s own mind. [No self] Not to take the physical body (the four great elements) as one’s own body or thoughts (the shadowy reflections of the six dusts) as one’s own mind, but to take the dharma-body as one’s own body and the numinous awareness as one’s own mind. [Setting the self in opposition to things] To take the self as the center and stand opposed to others. Here “things” means people other than oneself.

[Laozi has a saying: “The soft overcomes the hard; the weak overcomes the strong.” This is the first stage of the practice of patience. Sentient beings rely on their view of self, which is firm and hard to break; and so a single contrary word cannot be borne, a single contrary matter cannot be tolerated, a single hunger or cold cannot be endured, a single thought of desire cannot be purified — all because they do not know the method of patience, and only increase their clinging to the view of self! Therefore the Buddha taught his disciples to cultivate the practice of harmony. He also said: the patience of the truth of suffering, the wisdom of the truth of suffering. And he also said: the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is attained only at the eighth ground. From this we know that from the patience of dharmas as born, enduring on until no-birth, the wondrous practice is perfected and the Buddha-fruit accomplished! How could the single practice of patience be a shallow thing! Therefore it is said: in whatever you do, you should endure.]

The Daodejing of Laozi says: “The soft overcomes the hard; the weak overcomes the strong.” This is the first stage of the practice of patience. The view of self that sentient beings hold is firm and hard to break; and so a single contrary word cannot be borne, a single contrary matter cannot be tolerated, a single hunger or cold cannot be endured, a single thought of desire cannot be purified — all because they do not know the method of the practice of patience, and only keep strengthening their clinging to the view of self! Therefore the Buddha taught his disciples to cultivate the practice of harmony. He also says: “The patience of the truth of suffering, the wisdom of the truth of suffering.” And he also says: “The patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is realized only by a bodhisattva of the eighth ground.” From this we know that enduring on from the patience of dharmas as born until nirvāṇa (no-birth) is attained, the wondrous practice is perfected and the Buddha-fruit accomplished! How could the single practice of “patience” be a trifling matter! Therefore it is said: in whatever you do, you should be able to endure.

[View of self] Also called attachment to self. Falsely clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind as oneself. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have all kinds of inversions, like a deluded person who changes his directions (for example, taking east as west, south as north, and so on), falsely acknowledging the four great elements as the marks of their own body and the shadowy reflections of the six dusts as the marks of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good sons! The sky truly has no flowers; the diseased one falsely clings to them. Because of this false clinging, he is confused not only about the self-nature of this emptiness, but also about where the real flowers arise. Hence he falsely has the revolving of birth and death; this is called ignorance.” [Four great elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, wind has motion as its nature. All material forms in the world possess these four natures of hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion, and so are called “great.” [Shadowy reflections of the six dusts] The various thoughts produced when the six sense-faculties come into contact with the six dusts; and since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadowy reflections of the six dusts — the illusory shadows conditioned by the six dusts.

[A single contrary word cannot be borne, a single contrary matter cannot be tolerated, a single hunger or cold cannot be endured, a single thought of desire cannot be purified] This speaks of those who cannot be patient. Patience means being able to do this: to bear a contrary word, to tolerate a contrary matter, to endure hunger and cold, to purify desire when it arises.

[Harmony] Harmony is of two kinds: harmony in principle and harmony in affairs. Harmony in principle is the realization of cessation-by-choice — that is, all together cultivating and realizing this commonly chosen principle of quiescence. Harmony in affairs has six items, the so-called six reverent harmonies: 1. Harmony of body in dwelling together — peaceful coexistence of the body; 2. Harmony of speech in being without contention — speech that does not give rise to argument; 3. Harmony of mind in sharing joy — shared gladness of mind; 4. Harmony of precepts in cultivating together — common observance of the precepts; 5. Harmony of view in understanding alike — complete agreement of views; 6. Harmony of benefit in sharing equally — benefits enjoyed as one body. [The patience of the truth of suffering] With regard to the sufferings of the desire realm, the mind of wisdom abides in the principle of suchness. [The wisdom of the truth of suffering] The undefiled wisdom obtained by contemplating the truth of suffering in the desire realm. [The patience of dharmas as born] The various kinds of patience prior to the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas are called the patience of dharmas as born.

[Thus, wherever the mind stirs and a thought arises, test it with patience; wherever a foot is raised and a step taken, let patience go before; in every movement and every change of countenance, hold to patience; in joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, verify with patience. In this way the mind dares not stir wildly, the body dares not act wildly, in affairs one dares not do wildly, in feelings one dares not erupt wildly. Therefore Laozi says: “Not daring to be first in the world.” “Not daring” is another name for patience. Because of “not daring to be first in the world,” patience is the first practice for becoming Buddha.]

Therefore, wherever the mind stirs and a thought arises, examine it with patience; wherever a foot is raised and a step taken, let patience walk ahead; in dealing with people and handling matters, meet them with patience; in joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, test them with patience.

In this way the mind dares not stir wildly, the body dares not act wildly, in affairs one dares not do wildly, in feelings one dares not erupt wildly. Therefore Laozi says in the Daodejing: “Not daring to act willfully (at whim), one becomes the highest in the world.” “Not daring” is another name for patience. Since not daring (patience) is the highest in the world, patience is the foremost practice (the first practice) for becoming Buddha.
[Movement and turning] Bearing and conduct. [Change of countenance] The appearance of an expression on the face.

[In this way patience is great and the self is small; and so patience can clothe and cover me, and can also clothe and cover others. There is no virtue of benefiting self and others that surpasses this. Hence it is said, the robe of gentleness and patience — for this reason. The Chan practicer asked for a Dharma word, and so I have entitled it: Patience as a Robe. Let the Chan practicer strive to practice it; let him not take it as mere talk of the lips, and let him not use it to win himself a meal.]

In this way patience is great and the self is small; and so patience, like a warm garment in deep winter, can shelter me and can shelter others too. There is no virtue of benefiting self and others that surpasses patience. Hence the saying that one should take gentleness and patience as one’s robe — this is the very reason. The Chan practicer Fajin came to ask for a Dharma word, and so I have entitled this instruction: Patience as a Robe. Fajin, you must strive to practice it! Do not think it a commonplace, and do not use it as a tool to win fame and profit, but carry it out in your own person.

[Robe of patience] The mind of patience, because it can ward off all outer obstructions, is likened to a robe. [Talk of the lips] Set phrases always hanging on the lips. [Win] To exchange for. [Not to use it to win himself a meal] Master Hanshan here warns with weighty earnestness: to study and understand the principle is to practice it in one’s own person; one must never fail to do it oneself while using it to teach others, making it a tool to win fame and profit. The Analects

Xian Wen says: “The learning of the ancients was for themselves; the learning of people today is for others.” The Analects with Commentary and Sub-commentary says: “The learning of the ancients was to tread and practice it — this was for themselves. The learning of people today is merely to speak of it to others, while they cannot practice it themselves — this is for others. Fan Ye says: ‘To be for others is to display oneself to things by means of reputation; to be for oneself is to meet the Way by means of the mind.’” [To display oneself to things by means of reputation] To appear to others (things) by means of reputation — that is, to fish for fame and reputation. “Feng” is in ancient usage the same as “ping” — to rely on, to depend on. “Things” means people other than oneself.

blocks.text: 15. Shattering the Dream and Escaping the Peril

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Practicer Mingzhe)

[In the fourth year of my banishment, in the summer of the jǐhài year, I was lecturing on the New Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra in the Traveler’s Rest Hermitage at Qingmen in Wuyang. The Chan practicer came from several thousand li away to call on me in this land of miasma. Seeing his careful and honest manner, I appointed him to oversee the temple meals, intending thereby to let him know the three virtues and harmonize the six flavors, gathering in the one mind while cultivating the ten thousand practices. The Chan practicer obeyed my instructions in all things and worked diligently for more than half a year. Then he happened to breathe the miasmic vapors and was gradually infected with illness. He felt that the four great elements could no longer support him and that he could not bear the many duties. So he begged to cross north of the ranges and seek a pleasant place to rest and recover. When he came to take his leave, the old man therefore urged him, saying: Do you think that suffering and joy are different places, and that death and life have a here and a there? You do not realize that the four great elements are something borrowed, that suffering and joy are a stage of illusion, that death and life are night and morning; nor do you know that the mind is the source of all evils and the body the root of all suffering.]

In the fourth year of my banishment, in the summer of the jǐhài year, I was lecturing on the New Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra in the Traveler’s Rest Hermitage at Qingmen in Wuyang (Guangzhou). The Chan practicer Mingzhe came from several thousand li away to call on me in this land of miasma. Seeing his solid and honest manner, I appointed him to oversee the temple meals, and further instructed him, letting him understand that overseeing the meals, with the three virtues and the six flavors, is likewise gathering in the one mind while cultivating the ten thousand practices. The Chan practicer strictly followed my teaching and had worked diligently for more than half a year. Then, because of the miasma, he was gradually infected with illness. He felt that his physical body could no longer support him and that he could not bear the many duties. So he asked to go north of the ranges and seek a place of peace and comfort to rest and recover. He came to take his leave, and I therefore urged him, saying: How could you think that a land of suffering and a land of joy are different places, and that death and life have a this and a that? You do not realize at all that this is borrowing the four great elements for a body, that the land of suffering and the land of joy are an illusory stage, and that death and life are but the alternation of night and day upon that stage; nor do you know that the mind is the source of all evils and the body the root of all suffering.
[Land of miasma] A place in the south with miasmic vapors. [Miasma] The damp, hot, stifling vapor in the mountain forests of the tropics that causes people to fall ill. Abbreviated as
zhàng,” as in “zhàng-lì (miasmic fever),” “dú-zhàng (poisonous miasma),” “zhàng-yǔ mán-yān (miasmic rain and barbarian smoke).” [Careful and honest] Solid and plain; the character is read “
què”

, pronounced as in the word for “certain.” [Oversee] To be in charge of. [The three virtues and harmonizing the six flavors] When the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, the upāsakas prepared all kinds of food and drink for the Buddha and the Saṃgha; the food was sweet and fine, possessing the three virtues and six flavors. In later ages this became the offering verse recited at temple meals: “Three virtues, six flavors, offered to the Buddha and the Saṃgha; sentient beings of the Dharma realm, all equally receive the offering.” The three virtues: light and soft, pure and clean, in accord with the Dharma. The six flavors: bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland.

[Originally, because the mind was deluded it became consciousness, and one clung to the false as the body, inverting birth and death, appearing and disappearing in the path of suffering, for who knows how many thousands of ten-million kalpas. It is like racing through a perilous road in a dream, terrified and panicked, seeking escape and unable, wishing to get away and not permitted. Sorrowful and wretched, one looks for rescue with no door to turn to; the spirit is worn out, with no means of rest even for a moment. One thinks that one will at last fall into the depths, and so one resigns oneself to drowning. How could one know that by calling out with all one’s might and leaping up with a sudden start, one greatly awakens — and then all the former sorrow and bitterness become a laughingstock. Since one is now awake, how different that is from the former seeking of escape — as different as heaven from earth!]

Sentient beings originally, because they were deluded about the one mind and it became the eight consciousnesses, falsely cling to the four great elements as the body; and so they invert birth and death (taking the illusory as real), appearing and disappearing in the path of suffering, and no one knows for how many thousands of ten-million kalpas this has gone on. This is like racing through a perilous road in a dream, terrified and flustered, wishing to shake it off and unable, wishing to get away and not permitted. Sorrowful and wretched, one looks for rescue with no door to turn to; one can only flee with all one’s might, utterly exhausted, with no way even to catch one’s breath. Thinking there is no way out, one can only accept one’s fate. How could you know that if you but call out with all your might and leap up with a sudden start, the dream will be broken, and all the sorrow and bitterness of the dream will become a laughingstock. Comparing the joy of the nightmare now ended with the suffering of fleeing in the nightmare, there is truly the difference between heaven and hell!
[And so] Thereupon. [Drowning (gǔ)] To sink.

This passage says: sentient beings, from beginningless kalpas, have revolved in birth and death because of delusion and inversion, appearing and disappearing in the path of suffering. This is like having a nightmare: one thinks that these terrors and sufferings cannot be utterly escaped, and so one can only flee helplessly, and when one cannot flee, one can only endure. Yet one does not know that if one but cries out loudly and leaps up with a sudden start, the dream will break — what need then for fleeing and enduring? Once the dream is broken, you discover that all the terror in the dream, the suffering, and the resignation to enduring when rescue was sought in vain, were truly laughable. The joyous state of a mind at ease after waking, compared with the suffering state of desperately fleeing in the dream and enduring when escape was impossible — truly the difference between heaven and an abyss!
Therefore the way of liberation is not to dodge and flee this way and that within the dream of saṃsāra, but to wake from the deluded dream!

[Looking at it from your present state, this groaning in sickness and this thought of going or staying, of seeking release, are just like things in a dream. You cannot cry out yourself and wake; I cry out loudly for you, and still you do not know it. Then in this worn-out long night there will never be a time of opening your eyes. Why should you, for the sake of illusion and falsehood, be content with bitterness and toil, taking the dream house as your true home? Now that you have met with one who calls and still do not wake, if you abandon this, who else will call to you? Alas, alas! In the dark, inverted long night, to wish to see the light of the wisdom sun, with an opportunity such as today’s — that is difficult beyond difficulty! Try to think it over: if you suddenly rouse yourself, turn your head and shift your mind, and the pass of birth-and-death emotion bursts open at once, that is the time of shattering the dream house and escaping the perilous road.]

Judging by your present plan, this groaning in sickness, and this thought of going or staying (“going” meaning leaving this land of miasma and crossing north of the ranges; “staying” meaning finding another pleasant place to rest) and of seeking release (seeking to escape the suffering state of illness), are just like things in a dream. You cannot cry out loudly and wake up with a start yourself, and though I cry out loudly to wake you, you still do not know it. In this way you can only struggle wearily and helplessly through the long, long night, and there will never come a time when you open your eyes and wake. Why should you cling to the illusory state as real and be content to be tormented by it, taking the dream house as your true home? Now that you have met me crying out loudly to you and still do not wake, if you abandon this, who else will cry out to wake you? Alas, alas! In this dark, inverted, long, long night, to wish to see the light of the wisdom sun, with an opportunity such as today’s, is difficult beyond difficulty! Think it over carefully: if you suddenly rouse yourself, turn your head and shift your mind, then the pass of birth-and-death emotion bursts open at once, and this is the time of shattering the dream house and escaping the perilous road.
[Worn out (ěr)] Weary and exhausted. [Naihe] The same as the usual “naihe”; here it means: why.
(The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Practicer Shu Zhong’an on Dwelling in the Mountains)

[The Chan practicer Shu Zhong’an was about to clear the thatch on the Southern Peak and asked for the essentials of the Dharma for dwelling in the mountains. The old man therefore instructed him, saying: The Way is not in the mountains, yet to dwell in the mountains one must first see the Way. To see the mountain and forget the Way — the mountain becomes the root of obstruction. To see the Way and forget the mountain — wherever the eye falls and conditions are met, there is nothing that is not the Way. This is a famous saying of the ancient worthies and the true instruction of Yongjia. Now you intend to dwell in the mountains: is it that you will see the Way and then dwell, or dwell and afterwards see the Way? If you see the Way and then dwell, then in dwelling there is abiding, and where there is abiding the Way is not the true Way. If you wish to dwell in the mountains and afterwards see the Way — the Way is originally without abiding, and where there is abiding the Way is not in the mountain. What then will you take as the Way, and where will you dwell?]

The Chan practicer Shu Zhong’an was about to build a thatched hut on the Southern Peak to cultivate the Way, and asked for instruction on the essentials of dwelling in the mountains. The old man therefore instructed him, saying: The Way is not in the mountains, yet to dwell in the mountains one must first see the Way. To see the mountain and forget the Way — the mountain becomes the root of obstructing the Way. To see the Way and forget the mountain — wherever the eye falls and conditions are met, there is nothing that is not the Way. This is a famous saying of the ancient worthies and the true instruction of Master Yongjia. Now you intend to dwell in the mountains: will you see the Way and then dwell, or dwell and afterwards see the Way? If you see the Way and then go to dwell in the mountains, then in dwelling there is attachment, and where there is attachment the Way is not the true Way. If you wish to dwell in the mountains and afterwards see the Way — the Way is originally without attachment, and where there is attachment the Way is not in the mountains either. What then will you take as the Way, and where will you dwell?

[Clearing the thatch] That is, cutting away the cogongrass; by extension, building a hut and settling down to cultivate the Way. [Southern Peak] Also written with a variant character; one of the Five Peaks, namely Mount Heng, in the central part of Hunan Province.

[You alone take the mountain as a mountain, not realizing that in daily life before you, body, mind, and the objects of mind are all mountains. The teachings say: birth, old age, sickness, and death are pressed upon by four mountains. They also say: the mountain of the five aggregates; the mountain of self and others; the mountain of nirvāṇa. Yet nirvāṇa is the mind; self and others are the object; the five aggregates of body and mind are the den of birth, old age, sickness, and death. The Sanskrit word nirvāṇa is rendered here as “quiescent extinction.” The illusory body, mind, and objects of mind all belong to movement and disturbance; but tracing them to their root, the true and the false are not two, and movement and stillness are both suchness. It is only because of the division between delusion and awakening that there is the distinction between sage and ordinary being. Deluded, nirvāṇa becomes birth and death; awakened, birth and death realizes nirvāṇa. From this we know that the mountain of the five aggregates and of self and others is originally the peaceful abode of nirvāṇa. Thus all sages and ordinary beings, in birth and in death, have never failed to dwell on this mountain — and you have long been lying and dwelling upon it through the long night. Why then do you now wish to go and dwell in the mountains?]

You alone take the Southern Peak as a mountain, not realizing that in daily life before you, body, mind, and the objects of mind are all mountains. The teachings say: “Birth, old age, sickness, and death are pressed upon by four mountains.” They also say: “the mountain of the five aggregates”; “the mountain of self and others”; “the mountain of nirvāṇa.” Yet nirvāṇa is mind; self and others are object; the five aggregates of body and mind are the den of birth, old age, sickness, and death. The Sanskrit word “nirvāṇa” means in Chinese “quiescent extinction.” The illusory body, mind, and objects of mind all belong to movement and disturbance; tracing them to their source, the true and the false are not two, and movement and stillness are both suchness. It is only because of the division between delusion and awakening that there is the distinction between sage and ordinary being. Deluded, nirvāṇa becomes birth and death; awakened, birth and death realizes nirvāṇa. From this we know that the mountain of the five aggregates and of self and others is originally the peaceful abode of nirvāṇa. Therefore all sages and ordinary beings, in birth and in death, have never failed to dwell on this mountain of the five aggregates and of self and others; and you, lying and dwelling in the long night of saṃsāra, have been dwelling on this mountain all along — why then do you still wish to go and dwell in the mountains?

[If one takes delight and aversion, taking up and casting off, as the resources for entering the Way, that is like fleeing from drowning and throwing oneself into fire. Hence it is said: I wish to escape it, yet cannot escape; beyond the great square all is blocked and filled. It is also said: the mad mind does not rest; when it rests, that is bodhi. The essentials of entering the Way lie only in resting the mad mind, blotting out seeing and hearing, cutting off knowing and understanding, forgetting subject and object, stilling right and wrong, and quiescing this mind. It is not at all a matter of fleeing the body into mountain valleys, eating one’s fill and lying about, indulging in sloth and idleness, and increasing one’s arrogance, and taking that as the wonder of the Way. The Sanskrit word dhūta is rendered here as “shaking off,” because it can shake off the afflictions of guest-dust. To simply purify one’s mind — this is the Way of all Buddhas. Do strive after it.]

If one takes the mind of delight and aversion, of taking up and casting off, as the resource for entering the Way, that is like fleeing from drowning and throwing oneself into fire. Hence it is said: “I wish to escape it, yet cannot escape; beyond the great square all is blocked and filled.” It is also said: “The mad mind does not rest; when it rests, that is bodhi.” Therefore the essentials of entering the Way lie only in resting the mad mind, blotting out seeing and hearing, cutting off knowing and understanding, forgetting subject and object, stilling right and wrong, and quiescing this mind. It is precisely not a matter of fleeing the body into mountain valleys, eating one’s fill and lying about, indulging in sloth and idleness, and increasing one’s arrogance, while thinking this is the wonder of the Way. The Sanskrit word “dhūta” means in Chinese “shaking off,” because one is able to rouse the spirit and rid oneself of the afflictions of guest-dust. To simply purify one’s mind — this is the Buddha Way! May you practice it with diligence.

[I wish to escape it, yet cannot escape; beyond the great square all is blocked and filled] “The mad mind does not rest; when it rests, that is bodhi.” Therefore the essentials of entering the Way lie only in resting the mad mind, and not in fleeing the body into mountain valleys. If the mad mind does not rest, then even if you flee beyond the great earth, that place too is filled and blocked with affliction. The Song-dynasty monk Shi Chongxian, in his poem “Seeing Off the Chief Seat Shanxian,” says: “I fear that if I wish to escape it, I cannot escape; beyond the great square there is no outside, all is blocked and filled. Vast and chaotic, who knows where it ends; on every side the fragrant wind (the mood of extravagance and indulgence) catches the hem of the robe (the lapel).” [Great square] The ancients held that heaven is round and earth square, and so “great square” refers to the great earth.

blocks.text: 17. Only Detach from the Mind’s Defilement

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to Liu Cunchi)

The sūtra says: Ordinary beings, worthies, and sages are equal, with no higher or lower; it is only that the mind’s defilement is extinguished, and then the realization is attained as easily as turning over one’s palm.

[Recently I retired in my old age to the Southern Peak. At the end of winter in the jiǎyín year, Liu Jizi of Chaling came from afar to call and inquire. On a snowy night we sat around the stove, a cold lamp lighting us. I therefore asked him: How have you been applying your mind all along? He replied: Formerly I received your instruction, reverend sir, in a verse: “The lotus is born within the fire — the world calls this rare; yet it is not that fire gives birth to the lotus, but only that the mind is free of defilement.” Whenever I read these words, I gain much benefit from the last line. The old man was deeply pleased, and therefore instructed him, saying: That you have gained strength from the line “only that the mind is free of defilement” — these words are not empty, yet they are not easy to reach. The sūtra says: Ordinary beings, worthies, and sages are equal, with no higher or lower; it is only that the mind’s defilement is extinguished, and then the realization is attained as easily as turning over one’s palm.]

Not long ago, in my old age, I retired to the Southern Peak. At the end of winter in the jiǎyín year, Liu Cunchi of Chaling came from afar to call and inquire. The two of us sat around the stove on a snowy night, a cold lamp lighting us. So I asked him: How have you been applying your mind all along? He answered: “Formerly I received your instruction, reverend sir, in a verse: ‘The lotus is born within the fire — the world calls this rare; yet it is not that fire gives birth to the lotus, but only that the mind is free of defilement.’ Each time I read this verse, I gain much benefit from the last line, ‘only that the mind is free of defilement.’” Hearing this I was very glad, and therefore instructed him, saying: That you have gained strength from the line “the mind is free of defilement” — these words are true and substantial, yet also not easy to accomplish. The sūtra says: Ordinary beings, worthies, and sages are equal, with no higher or lower; it is only that the mind’s defilement is extinguished, and then the realization is attained as easily as turning over one’s palm.

[Reverend sir] Meaning “my teacher”; it is the honorific used by monks for their own preceptor. [The lotus is born within the fire, the world calls this rare; yet it is not that fire gives birth to the lotus, but only that the mind is free of defilement] A lotus growing out of fire is thought by worldly people to be exceedingly rare and precious; yet what is rarest and most precious is not a lotus born in fire, but the mind’s freedom from illusory defilement.
[From
(in ancient usage written with the character for “you”)

this we see: sentient beings and Buddhas are originally not two; as it is said, mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction. But when the mind is pure, that is Buddha; when the mind is defiled, that is sentient being. The distance between sentient being and Buddha is not far; it lies only in whether the mind’s defilement is extinguished or not. Because this mind is originally pure, and only through craving, anger, delusion, arrogance, the five desires, and afflictions — all kinds of karmic illusions — is it obscured by defilement and turbidity, it is therefore called a sentient being. If this defilement is purified, one is then called a Buddha — how could this depend on any other power!]

From this we see: sentient beings and Buddhas are originally not two; as it is said, mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction. Only, when the mind is pure one is a Buddha; when the mind is defiled one is a sentient being. The road by which sentient beings become Buddhas is not far; it lies only in whether the mind’s defilement is extinguished or not. Because this mind is originally pure, and only through craving, anger, delusion, arrogance, the five desires, and other afflictions — all kinds of illusory karma — is it obscured by defilement and turbidity, it is therefore called a sentient being. If this defilement is purified, one is then called a Buddha — how could this depend on any other power!

[Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction] Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings: these three dharmas are fundamentally without distinction. When the mind is pure (the mind is purified), this mind is Buddha; when the mind is defiled (the mind is tainted), this mind is sentient being. [Affliction] “Fan” means to disturb, “nao” means to disorder; whatever can disturb the body and mind of sentient beings and make the mind fretful and confused is called “affliction.” There are six root afflictions: craving, anger, delusion, arrogance, doubt, and wrong view. Craving is craving for the five desires; anger is wrath without forbearance; delusion is foolish ignorance; arrogance is haughty self-importance; doubt is suspicious misgiving; wrong view is incorrect views, including the view of the body, the extreme view, deviant view, the view of grasping views, and the view of grasping precepts. Craving, anger, delusion, arrogance, and doubt, together with the five wrong views, make ten root afflictions, also called the ten delusions or the ten messengers. Craving, anger, delusion, arrogance, and doubt are called delusions of thought; the five wrong views are called delusions of view. Together they are called the delusions of view and thought, or the afflictions of view and thought. [Ten messengers] Also called the ten delusions, or the ten root afflictions: 1. Craving — craving for the five desires; 2. Anger — wrath without forbearance; 3. Delusion — foolish ignorance; 4. Arrogance — haughty self-importance; 5. Doubt — suspicious unbelief; 6. View of the body — clinging to the five aggregates as the root body; 7. Extreme view — clinging to the two views of permanence and annihilation; 8. Deviant view — denying cause and effect, destroying all good works; 9. The view of grasping views — holding to one’s own opinion, taking the non-fruit as fruit; 10. The view of grasping precepts — holding to incorrect precepts, taking the non-cause as cause. The first five are called the five dull messengers, the latter five the five sharp messengers. “Messenger” is another name for affliction, because affliction can cause sentient beings to fall into birth and death.

[But there is no help for it: all sentient beings have deep and heavy karmic obstructions from beginningless time, and firm afflictions, and it is hard for them to attain purity; they must rely on the work of polishing and refining. Hence there are Chan investigation, Buddha-recitation, huatou-contemplation, and various other skillful means — all of them medicines for treating the mind. For example, the light of a mirror is originally bright, but because of grime it is dimmed, and it must rely on the medicine of polishing. Yet the medicine is itself grime; because it is used to remove the grime, when the mirror is bright the medicine is no longer there. Again, when true gold is in the ore, with sand and stone and filth, there must be a method of smelting; when the gold is pure, the smelting is no longer needed. The mind’s defilement of sentient beings is hard to detach from, and one must work with diligence and refine and treat it; when the defilement is gone and the mind is bright, it is said that sentient beings are originally Buddhas — not that while dwelling all along amid the turbidity of affliction one may recklessly call oneself a Buddha.]

There is no help for it: all sentient beings, from beginningless kalpas, have deep and heavy karmic obstructions and firm afflictions, and it is hard for them to attain purity; they must rely on the work of polishing and refining. Hence there are Chan investigation, Buddha-recitation, huatou-contemplation, and various other skillful means — all of them medicines for treating the mind. For example, the light of a mirror is originally bright; because of grime it is dimmed, and it must rely on the medicine of polishing (in ancient times bronze mirrors were polished with a polishing compound to remove grime). Yet the medicine is itself grime; it is used only because it can remove the grime. Therefore, when the mirror is bright the medicine is no longer used. Again, when true gold is in the ore, the sand, stone, and filth must be removed before pure gold can be obtained, and so a method of smelting must be used. Once the pure gold has been refined, the method of smelting is no longer used. Because the mind’s defilement of sentient beings is firm and hard to detach from, one must work at it, refining and treating it with diligence. When the defilement is gone and the mind is bright, the work too need no longer be done; and so it is said that sentient beings are originally Buddhas. It is not that while dwelling all along amid the turbidity of affliction one may recklessly call oneself a Buddha.

[The one path of Chan investigation and huatou-contemplation is the most essential for illuminating the mind, yet in recent times those who take it in hand are few. On the one hand, their faculties are dull, and they lack the death-ground resolve of the ancients; on the other, they have no true spiritual benefactor to decide and select for them, and most fall into deviant views. Therefore the practice of cultivating Buddha-recitation and Chan investigation together is an extremely reliable Dharma gate. If one takes a single sound of Buddha-recitation and stores it in the breast, thought after thought pursuing and verifying where it arises and where it falls, determined to see a precise landing place — after a long, long time, suddenly the defilement is purified and brightness appears, and the mind-ground opens through. This is no different from contemplating a koan or huatou, and one must press on with unremitting effort to succeed. If one drifts up and down on delusive thoughts and passes the days idly, taking this as a matter of no importance, then to the end of one’s years one will gain no benefit. If one takes idly letting delusive thoughts run as one’s benefit, then one deceives oneself — not merely for this one life: from now on, even to the end of kalpas, there will be no time when one is not deceived.]

The one path of Chan investigation and huatou-contemplation is the most essential for illuminating the mind (removing the mind’s defilement), yet in recent times those who can take it in hand are very few. On the one hand this is because their faculties are dull and they lack the death-ground resolve of the ancients; on the other hand it is because they have no true spiritual benefactor to guide them correctly, and most fall into deviant views. Therefore the practice of cultivating Buddha-recitation and Chan investigation together (the investigation of Buddha-recitation) is an extremely reliable Dharma gate. Its method is: recite one sound of the Buddha’s name and store it in the breast, pursuing and verifying where the Buddha-name arises and where it falls, thought after thought, determined to see a precise landing place. After a long time, suddenly the defilement is purified and brightness appears, and the mind-ground opens through. This is no different from the Chan school’s contemplation of a koan or huatou, and one must press on with dense and unremitting effort. If one drifts up and down on delusive thoughts and passes the days idly, taking this investigation of Buddha-recitation as a matter of no importance, then one will gain no benefit in a whole lifetime. If one takes idly letting delusive thoughts run as one’s benefit, then one deceives oneself — not merely in this life: from now on, even to the end of kalpas, there will be no time when one is not deceived.
[This is no different from contemplating a koan or huatou] This is no different from the Chan school’s contemplation of a koan or huatou. In the Dream-Wandering Collection

Instructions to the Chan Practicer Zhaofan Yong, Master Hanshan says: “It is like the monk asking Zhaozhou whether a dog has the Buddha-nature; or like Yongming teaching people to verify who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. This one word ‘no’ or this one word ‘who’ is precisely the sharp sword that cuts off the life-root of birth and death. Yet this investigation and verification is only a matter of peering at this word ‘no’ or ‘who’ — from where does it arise, and to where does it fall? Just watch where this single thought arises and falls, and you must see the root of its arising and ceasing. If you investigate to the ultimate point, you will burst apart the delusive thoughts of a single thought’s arising and ceasing, smash the lacquer barrel, and suddenly see your original face.” (For details see
Investigating Buddha-Recitation
) [Pressing close] Closely arrayed. Here it means doing the work densely and with unremitting effort.

[You have long had a karmic affinity with the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation; try to investigate and verify it in earnest. If, amid the defilement and turbidity of affliction, a single sound of the Buddha-name is like a water-clearing pearl, then you gain benefit from it — but this is not yet a thoroughgoing penetration to the source. The sūtra says: It is like settling turbid water; the sand and earth sink of themselves, and clear water appears — this is called first subduing the afflictions of guest-dust. When the mud is gone and the water is pure, this is called forever cutting off fundamental ignorance. Do but test this Buddha-word silently for yourself, and there will be no failure. If you reach the place of true freedom from defilement, then, as the sūtra says, the mark of brightness is pure and undefiled, and one is no longer obstructed by the afflictions of guest-dust. In that way, not only will Amitābha come to receive and guide you, but the Buddhas of the ten directions will all praise you with one voice!]

You have long had a karmic affinity with the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation; simply recite with this method of earnest investigation and verification. When the work is deep, then amid the defilement and turbidity of affliction, a single sound of the Buddha-name is like a water-clearing pearl: as soon as the Buddha-name is raised, delusive thoughts all vanish. In this way you gain considerable benefit — but this is not yet a thoroughgoing penetration to the source. The sūtra says: “It is like settling turbid water; the sand and earth sink of themselves (the same as ‘sink’), and clear water appears — this is called first subduing the afflictions of guest-dust. When the mud is gone and the water is pure, this is called forever cutting off fundamental ignorance.” Do but test this passage of the Buddha’s words silently for yourself, and there will be no failure. If you reach the place of true freedom from defilement, then, as the sūtra says: “The mark of brightness is pure and undefiled, and one is no longer obstructed by the afflictions of guest-dust.” Having reached this state, not only will Amitābha Buddha come to receive and guide you, but the Buddhas of the ten directions will all praise you with one voice!

[Water-clearing pearl] The Threefold Recitation of Zhongfeng says: “In the Western Heaven there is a treasure called the clearing pearl. It is said that when this pearl is thrown into turbid water, for every inch it enters, an inch of the turbid water at once becomes clean. As this pearl enters the water, from inch to foot, even to the bottom, the turbid water becomes clear and limpid along with it. You should know that the clearing pearl is a simile for the pure thought of Buddha-recitation; the turbid water is a simile for the confused and deluded mind.”

[Happily I have spent with you the year’s end and a snowy night, and this plain and cool family style is rare in the world. If you do not betray this fine gathering, then from now on, never parting from it thought after thought, in this plainness and coolness there is a path of freedom from defilement. Press on with effort at every step, and there will surely come a time of reaching home and true liberation.]
I am very glad to have spent with you, at the year’s end and on this snowy night, this stretch of
plain
and cool
family style, which is rare in the world. If you would not betray this fine gathering, then from now on you must not part from it thought after thought; investigate and verify in earnest, and
in that plainness
and coolness
there is a shortcut to freedom from the mind’s defilement. Press on with effort at every step of the work, and there will surely come a time of reaching home and true liberation.
[“Líng”
(líng)
] Cool and refreshing. [“Líng
dàn”
] Cool, quiet, and plain.
(The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to Dong Zhiguang)

Delusive thought is the cause of all karma; if one is not driven by delusive thought, there is no cause of karma-making. If one can sever it with a single thought at the place where delusive thought arises, then the long-accumulated root of karma is dissolved on the spot.

[The student Dong Sizhang grew up in a house of wealth and honor, and early aroused the mind that seeks to escape birth and death — this is the power of the inner permeation of the supreme condition of prajñā cultivated in former lives. He first called on Master Yunqi, who taught him the Pure Land Dharma gate. Recently he called on the old man at Shuangjing and wished to receive the upāsaka precepts. He further disclosed that his karmic offenses were deep and heavy, and wished to learn the essentials of escaping suffering: by what cultivation should he extinguish his transgressions? The old man therefore instructed him, saying:]

Dong Sizhang grew up in a house of wealth and honor and early aroused the mind to escape birth and death — this is the power of the inner permeation of the supreme condition of prajñā cultivated in former lives. He first called on Master Lianchi, who taught him the Pure Land Dharma gate. Not long after, he came to call on me at Shuangjing and wished to receive the upāsaka precepts. He further disclosed that his karmic offenses were deep and heavy, and wished to learn the essentials of escaping suffering: how should he cultivate in order to extinguish his transgressions? Therefore I instructed him, saying:

[Upāsaka precepts] “Upāsaka” means a male lay devotee. The upāsaka precepts are the five precepts: not to kill, not to steal, not to commit sexual misconduct, not to speak falsely, and not to drink alcohol.

[Since the student knows that the root of his transgressions is deep and heavy — the ancient worthies teach people: “At all times dissolve old karma; on no account create new calamity.” For sentient beings heavy in karma, the Buddha opened the one gate of repentance, which is the most skillful means of escaping suffering. The verse says: “All transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark.” This is the primary practice; all else is auxiliary skillful means.]

The ancient worthies teach people: “At all times dissolve old karma; on no account create new calamity.” The one gate of repentance that the Buddha opened for sentient beings heavy in karma is the most skillful means of escaping suffering. The verse says: “All transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark (the later text says, ‘the mind that has no thing is the true mark’).” This is the primary practice; all else is auxiliary practice.

[All transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them] Just as the sun melts frost and dew, so contemplating the true mark (the wisdom sun) can dissolve all transgressions. The Sūtra of the Method of Contemplating Bodhisattva Samantabhadra says:

“The sea of all karmic obstructions arises entirely from delusive thought. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark. All transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them.”
[Sea of karmic obstructions] Karmic obstructions as deep and vast as the great ocean. [Sit upright and contemplate the true mark] The later text says:
“The mind that has no thing — this is the true mark.”

[The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to the Buddha’s, originally undefiled, and without the marks of birth and death, coming and going. But because of the initial non-awakening, one is deluded about one’s own self-nature — hence it is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, all delusive thoughts arise, with every kind of inversion, creating every kind of karma and falsely seizing the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All this is ignorance: not understanding one’s own mind, one turns with delusive thought. It is like a person deep asleep having all kinds of evil dreams — every kind of state, every kind of terror, every kind of suffering hard to bear. When he wakes, he seeks the things of the dream and cannot find them at all. Therefore sentient beings fall into the dream of ignorance, follow delusive thought and inversion, create all kinds of karma, and seize all kinds of suffering for themselves. Seen with awakened eyes, how could those inverted states be had?]

The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to the Buddha’s, originally without defilement, and without the marks of birth and death, coming and going. But because of the initial non-awakening, one is deluded about one’s own self-nature (entering the dream of ignorance) — this is ignorance. Because of ignorance, all delusive thoughts arise, and so with every kind of inversion one creates every kind of karma and falsely seizes the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All this is ignorance: not awakening to one’s own mind, one is turned along by delusive thought. It is like a person in deep sleep having all kinds of evil dreams — every kind of state, every kind of terror, suffering beyond bearing. When he wakes, he seeks the things of the dream and cannot find them at all. Sentient beings are the same: fallen into the dream of ignorance, they follow delusive thought and inversion, create all kinds of karma, and seize all kinds of suffering for themselves. Seen with awakened eyes, where are all those inverted states?

[Now, while present in the dream of ignorance, how can one dissolve old karma? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and firmly believe that one’s own mind is originally pure, and not be driven by delusive thought and inversion; then all karma is without cause, because delusive thought is the cause of all karma. Why is this so? Because from beginningless time one has been deluded about one’s own original mind, and life after life has created all kinds of karma with the delusive mind. The habitual tendencies of that karma accumulate within the field of the eighth consciousness, and are irrigated with the water of ignorance, causing those evil seeds to put forth the sprouts of karma — this is the root of transgression, from which all evil karma arises.]

Then, now that one is already in the dream of ignorance, how can old karma be dissolved? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and firmly believe that one’s own mind is originally pure, and not be driven by delusive thought and inversion; in this way there is no cause of karma-making, because delusive thought is the cause of all karma. Why is this so? Because from beginningless kalpas one has been deluded about one’s own original mind, and life after life has created all kinds of karma with the delusive mind. These karmic habits accumulate in the ālaya consciousness (the eighth consciousness), and are then irrigated with the water of ignorance, causing those evil seeds to put forth the sprouts of karma — this is the root of transgression, from which all evil karma arises.

[Now, if one wishes to dissolve old karma, one must first arouse the great light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and not permit delusive thoughts to sprout and quietly grow in the dark. If one can sever them with a single thought at the place where delusive thought arises, then the long-accumulated root of karma is dissolved on the spot. As it is said: do not fear the arising of a thought; fear only that awareness comes late. If awareness and illumination are even slightly late, one is turned about by it. If one can, in daily life, at every place where the mind stirs and a thought arises, become aware of each thought and dissolve each thought, this is what is called “all transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them.” Since the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, this is called wisdom’s dissolving them.]

Now, if one wishes to dissolve old karma, one must first arouse the great light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and not permit delusive thoughts to sprout and quietly grow in the dark. If one can sever them with a single thought at the place where delusive thought arises (a chilling moment of awareness), then the root of karma accumulated in former days is dissolved on the spot. As it is said, “Do not fear the arising of a thought; fear only that awareness comes late.” If awareness and illumination are even slightly late, one is turned about by it (delusive thought). If one can, in daily life, at every place where the mind stirs and a thought arises, become aware of each thought and dissolve each thought, this is what is called “all transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them.” Since the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, this is what is meant by wisdom’s dissolving all transgressions.

[If, day and night without letting go, one diligently observes and does not let it pass, but simply, at the place where delusive thought arises, investigates exhaustively until there is no mark of arising at all — looking and looking again, in the end it cannot be found. When after a long time one is thoroughly familiar with this, then one’s own mind is pure and without thing; and the mind that has no thing is the true mark. If one constantly contemplates this mind, what delusive thought can be admitted, what accumulated karma can lodge there? Applying the mind in this way is called the samādhi of contemplation.]

You must, day and night without letting go, diligently observe and not let it pass, but simply, at the place where delusive thought arises, investigate exhaustively until there is no mark of arising at all. Looking and looking again, delusive thought in the end cannot be found at all. When after a long time you are thoroughly familiar with this, then your own mind is pure and without thing, and the mind that has no thing is the true mark. If you constantly contemplate this pure mind, what delusive thought can be admitted, what accumulated karma can lodge there? Applying the mind in this way is called the samādhi of contemplation.

[“If, day and night without letting go, one diligently observes”] Here “if” (ruò) means “you.” For example: “Change your duty of catching snakes, restore your taxes — what would you think of that?” (This line comes from Liu Zongyuan’s “The Snake-Catcher’s Discourse”; the meaning is: if one changed your job of catching poisonous snakes and restored your tax levy, what would you think of it?)

[If one’s own afflictions are coarse and heavy, and at the places where ignorance obstructs one is not aware of it — in such a case the ancient worthies had a method of investigation they taught people: take the koan of verifying Buddha-recitation and apply your strength there. Raise a single sound of the Buddha-name and set it across your breast, and at once investigate: who, after all, is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Thus, as you raise it you investigate it, never letting it go empty. Set this mass of doubt across your breast, like your own life-root, and never let it go. In all movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, coming and going, sitting and standing, there is only this one matter and nothing else. Applying the mind in this way, as soon as you see a delusive thought arise, give the huatou a single thrust, and it is shattered on the spot; all delusive thoughts of themselves are swept away without trace. For this huatou is like the sun’s disc in the sky, illuminating every dark place. The only fear is that one’s mental strength slackens and one will not earnestly rouse oneself, and so cannot stand against delusive thoughts. If one can stand against them, then where delusive thoughts vanish is the time when old karma is dissolved. Abandon this one stroke and seek elsewhere outside the mind, and even if all the Buddhas were to appear in the world, there would be no place for repentance. This rests on one’s own power; no other power can substitute for it.]

If one’s own afflictions are coarse and heavy, and at the places where ignorance obstructs (when delusive thoughts arise) one is unable to be aware of it — if this is one’s situation, then the ancient worthies had a method of investigation they taught people: take the koan of verifying Buddha-recitation (who is it that recites the Buddha’s name) and use it to cut off delusive thoughts. The method is: raise a single sound of the Buddha-name and set it across your breast, then at once investigate: who, after all, is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Thus, as you raise it you investigate it, never letting it go empty. Set this mass of doubt across your breast, like your own life-root, and never let it go. In all movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, coming and going, sitting and standing, there is only this one matter and nothing else. Only by applying the mind in this way, as soon as you see a delusive thought arise, do you give the huatou a single thrust, and delusive thought is shattered on the spot. Investigating in this way, all delusive thoughts of themselves are swept away without trace. For this huatou is like the sun’s disc in the sky, illuminating every dark place. The only fear is that one’s mental strength slackens and one will not earnestly rouse and hold to it, and therefore cannot stand against delusive thoughts. If one can stand against them, then where delusive thoughts vanish is the time when old karma is dissolved. Abandon this one stroke and seek elsewhere outside the mind, and then even if all the Buddhas were to appear in the world, there would be no place for repentance. This matter depends entirely on one’s own effort; no other power can substitute for it.

[Rousing and holding] To rouse oneself and bestir oneself, to keep right mindfulness. It also refers to concentrating on the work of investigation while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. The Gateless Gate of the Chan School says: “Take the three hundred and sixty bones and joints and the eighty-four thousand hair-pores, raise a mass of doubt through the whole body, and investigate the word ‘no,’ rousing and holding it day and night.” The Complete Works of Master Zhu

Preserving and Nourishing says: “One need only constantly rouse and hold it oneself; accumulating little by little, after a long time it will naturally continue without interruption and be beaten into one piece.” For example, the monk Ruiyan every day used to ask himself: “Master! Are you clear and awake?” and then answer himself: “I am clear and awake.” [Clear and awake] Alert and clear-minded.

[If evil habits are strong and one’s strength cannot stand against them, then formerly the Buddha gave a clear instruction: if a cultivator’s habitual tendencies are not removed, he should single-mindedly recite the heart-mantra spoken by me, the unconditioned Mind-Buddha. This is truly an extraordinary skillful means. Because each person’s storehouse consciousness flows on hidden currents, and habitual tendencies are deep and thick, the power of wisdom does not reach there. Where it does not reach, one must rely on the Buddha’s mind-seal to break through it secretly. It is like a bandit hard to subdue: one must request the imperial sword. For this, one should take the two periods of morning and evening, arrange them as suits one’s convenience, and recite the set lesson. In sum, the work of investigation is to be taken as the primary principle.]

If evil habits are strong and investigation cannot stand against delusive thoughts, then formerly the Buddha gave a clear instruction: “If a cultivator finds it hard to uproot his habitual tendencies, he should single-mindedly recite the heart-mantra spoken by me, the unconditioned Mind-Buddha.” This is truly an extraordinary skillful means. Because each person’s storehouse consciousness flows on hidden currents, and habitual tendencies are deep and thick, the power of wisdom does not reach there. Where it does not reach, one must rely on the Buddha’s mind-seal to break through it secretly. It is like a bandit hard to subdue: one must request the imperial sword.
